claims.text: Unmodified TC4 has an alpha-plus-beta dual-phase microstructure.
TC4 has relatively low surface hardness and inadequate wear resistance.
The proposed intervention is laser cladding a Ni60-Ti-Cu-B4C-CeO2 composite coating containing approximately 8 wt% B4C and 3 wt% CeO2 onto TC4.
The proposed laser-cladded coating will enhance TC4 surface hardness and wear resistance.
The coating will not compromise TC4's inherent beneficial properties.
The coating's benefits apply under simulated high-contact stress from room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures.
Laser cladding forms a refined composite microstructure containing finely distributed hard phases, eutectic structures, and solid solutions.
The refined phases impede dislocation motion and improve surface load support.
Rapid heating and cooling during laser cladding promote grain refinement and the formation of intermetallic and reinforced phases.
B4C particles contribute intrinsic hardness to the coating.
CeO2 causes microstructural refinement and phase stabilization.
The proposed microstructural changes raise hardness while reducing friction and wear.
The treated surface will have approximately 3.4 to 3.5 times the microhardness of untreated TC4.
The treated surface will have a friction coefficient approximately 30% to 35% lower than untreated TC4.
The treated surface will exhibit substantially lower wear volume than untreated TC4.
The treatment will retain the bulk toughness and corrosion resistance of TC4.
Untreated TC4 has a microhardness of approximately 320 HV.
Untreated TC4 has higher friction and greater wear than the proposed coated material under comparable tests.
Long-term coating adhesion and durability under cyclic mechanical and thermal loading remain uncertain.
The hypothesis is designated as falsified if coated specimens fail both to reach three times the control hardness and to reduce friction coefficient and wear volume by approximately 30% to 35%.
